d.1:2:
Creates an iterator of `KeyBinding` which represents all action+keystrokes in this collection bound to the same key-context.
This sequence can be provided to `App::bind_keys`, and any elements which use the same `InteractiveElement::key_context` will receive the bound actions.
d.1:3:
Returns one [`KeyBinding`] for each action and keystroke in the collection, all in `context`.

Pass `None` for `context` to make the bindings apply everywhere. Elements that declare a
matching [`key_context`](crate::InteractiveElement::key_context) receive the actions.
The order of the bindings is unspecified, because the collection is a hash map keyed by
action type. Bindings for different actions on the same keystrokes therefore have no
defined precedence.

# Panics

Panics if a keystroke fails to parse, or if `context` is not a valid key context
predicate.

Adds `keystrokes` as a trigger for the action type `A`, and returns the collection.

The action is built with `A::default()` once per type, so `A` must be a type you can
construct with `Default`, such as an action declared with [`actions!`](crate::actions).
Keystrokes aren't parsed here. They are parsed by [`as_keybindings`](Self::as_keybindings),
which panics on an invalid one.

Call this once per frame. After a run finishes, the sample returns its final value with

run starts, sampling returns the last settled value.

The run begins at `now`, using `motion`, and starts from the value on screen at that
moment. Returns `true` if the target changed. Setting the current target again returns
`false` and leaves the run alone.

Reverse-first playback flips motion progress into anchor-to-target progress. A custom
easing curve that starts away from zero can still cause an initial jump.

Elements that use it stay in step with each other. An element that mounts later joins the
shared phase, rather than starting from zero.

Caps re-renders at `max_fps` per second, using a timer between frames.

A value that is not finite or not positive is ignored, and the animation re-renders on every
frame.

Runs the prepaint phase with `origin` as the element's origin, in window coordinates.

Call [`AnyElement::layout_as_root`] first, or use [`AnyElement::prepaint_as_root`], which
does both. Returns the focus handle of a focused element in the subtree that became focused
during this call, if any.

d.1:3:
Returns this view as an element with a fixed root layout style.

GPUI can reuse the rendered subtree while the view's entity, tracked entity and global
reads, and layout environment remain unchanged. Reads made by nested views and deferred
prepaint or paint work are tracked too. A notification to a tracked entity, a tracked
global revision change, or [`Window::refresh`] causes the view to rebuild. Changes to
bounds or inherited layout and paint state can also require fresh output.

`style` sets the retained root's layout style. Pass the entity directly as a child when it
should keep its natural layout. See [`Entity::cached`] and
[retained view rendering](crate::_documentation::concepts::retained_rendering).

d.1:3:
Asserts that the entity this handle refers to has been released.

Use this in tests to find a strong handle that was leaked. A task or a subscription that still holds
a strong handle makes the check fail. The check needs the leak detector, which is enabled in tests
and with the `leak-detection` feature.

GPUI releases an entity when the update that dropped its last handle finishes. Run an update before
you call this, as the example does.

# Examples

```
# use gpui::{AppContext, TestApp};
# struct Document;
# let mut app = TestApp::new();
let document = app.update(|cx| cx.new(|_cx| Document));
let weak = document.downgrade();
drop(document);

// The update finishes, and GPUI releases the entity.
app.update(|_cx| {});
weak.assert_released();
```

# Debugging Leaks

If this method panics because of a leaked handle, set the `LEAK_BACKTRACE` environment variable to
see where the handle was created:
With leak detection enabled (build with `GPUI_LEAK_DETECTION=1`), a failure
lists each leaked handle. Also set the `LEAK_BACKTRACE` environment variable
to see where they were allocated:

```bash
GPUI_LEAK_DETECTION=1 LEAK_BACKTRACE=1 cargo test my_test
```

# Panics

- Panics if any strong handles to the entity are still alive.
- Panics if the entity was dropped in the current update. Its resources are kept until that update
  finishes.
